clue.text: He got profit from opposing 9 immigration

definitions.note: a phrase describing a person: one who opposed the Norman arrival

blocks.note: taken as written
a profit or return earned is a reward

explanation.surface: Someone made money by resisting immigrants, as if cashing in on hostility to newcomers.
explanation.walkthrough: 9 is NORMAN. Hereward the Wake led English resistance to the Norman Conquest in the Fens after 1066.
explanation.definitionFit: Hereward was the Saxon rebel famous for holding out against William the Conqueror's invading forces.

clue.text: Bow could be sinister

definitions.note: the word can be followed by sinister, in the heraldic term

blocks.note: first meaning: to bow is to stoop or curve
second meaning: in heraldry a diagonal band, which may run sinister (from the bearer's left)

explanation.walkthrough: A bend sinister is a heraldic stripe running from the shield's upper left (as the bearer sees it), popularly a mark of illegitimacy.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both a verb for stooping or curving and a heraldic stripe that may be dexter or sinister.

clue.text: Girl is first 7

blocks.note: taken as written
7 is DECEASED; Abel was the first man to die, killed by Cain

explanation.surface: A girl is the first one to have died, a grim little statement.
explanation.walkthrough: The cross-reference 7 points to 7-across, DECEASED; in Genesis Abel is the first person recorded as dying.
explanation.definitionFit: Isabel is a female given name, so it stands for a girl in crossword fashion.

clue.text: Top-liner trained to fight crime?

definitions.note: a description of the organisation's purpose, standing for its name

indicators.note: training reshapes something, so the preceding letters are put into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written, hyphen ignored

explanation.surface: A star performer has been schooled to take on criminals, like a celebrity turned crime-fighter.
explanation.definitionFit: Interpol is the international police organisation that coordinates efforts against cross-border criminals.

clue.text: His plain language leads to court order

definitions.text: His plain language leads to court order
definitions.note: the whole clue describes the lawyer who brings a case

indicators.note: putting something in order rearranges it, so the preceding word's letters are shuffled

blocks.note: prose is ordinary language, as opposed to verse
taken as written

explanation.surface: A lawyer's straight talking ends in a judge's ruling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leads to' puts the prose first, and 'court order' looks like a legal phrase but means the letters of court rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A prosecutor states the case against the accused in plain terms and seeks an order from the court.

clue.text: Al Gore gathered in abundance

indicators.note: things gathered up are bundled together in no set order, so the name's letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the politician's name taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: The American politician Al Gore collected plenty, perhaps votes or awards.
explanation.definitionFit: Galore is a postpositive adjective meaning in great quantity, plentifully, as in 'prizes galore'.

clue.text: Indeed a complicated case gets passed over

indicators.note: a complicated thing is tangled up, so the letters of the next word are jumbled

blocks.note: read as two words, in deed: the word deed, with in saying it goes around what follows
taken as written

explanation.surface: A tricky legal case gets ignored or set aside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Indeed' must be read as two words, in deed, to find the container; 'passed over' means died, not overlooked.
explanation.definitionFit: To pass over is a euphemism for dying, so someone who has passed over is dead.

clue.text: Bound up with the church in fraud

indicators.note: in a down entry going up means the word is written from bottom to top
having something in places it within the other letters

blocks.note: bound means tied up
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: Someone tied up with church affairs turns out to be involved in a swindle.
explanation.definitionFit: Deceit is dishonest trickery, the misleading of others for gain, which is what fraud amounts to.

clue.text: Baptismal name(s) given to an invader

blocks.note: first meaning: a man's given name, and also a surname
second meaning: one of the people who conquered England in 1066

explanation.surface: A christening name bestowed upon a foreign conqueror.
explanation.walkthrough: The '(s)' allows for both a first name and a surname.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is a common male first name and also names a member of the conquering people from Normandy.

clue.text: A joint for Tuesday?

definitions.note: a first name standing for the surname that goes with it

blocks.note: first meaning: a join made by fusing metal
second meaning: the surname of the American actress Tuesday ...

explanation.walkthrough: It reads like a cannabis joint saved for a weekday; Tuesday is the actress Tuesday Weld.
explanation.definitionFit: A weld is a seam formed by melting metal pieces together, and Weld is the actress's surname.

clue.text: Doctor Spock, but he may enable you to get off cheaply

definitions.text: may enable you to get off cheaply
definitions.note: the clue's 'he' makes it a description of the cut-price dealer

indicators.note: to doctor something is to tamper with it, so the letters that follow are altered in order

blocks.note: taken as written, ignoring punctuation

explanation.surface: Dr Spock, the childcare guru, may help you get away lightly.
explanation.walkthrough: Doctor Spock looks like a name, but 'Doctor' is the anagram signal; 'get off' means fly off on holiday, not escape punishment.
explanation.definitionFit: A bucket shop is an agency selling discounted airline tickets, so it helps travellers fly away for less.

clue.text: Male ideal raised on the farm

definitions.note: an adjective phrase standing for the crop it describes

blocks.note: M is the abbreviation for male
an angel is an ideal, perfect person

explanation.surface: A man's ideal grew up on a farm, a sweetheart from the countryside.
explanation.walkthrough: A mangel, or mangel-wurzel, is a large beet grown as cattle feed.
explanation.definitionFit: The mangel is a root vegetable cultivated by farmers as fodder for livestock, so it is grown on farms.

clue.text: A knot to tie - it was an investment

blocks.note: a granny is a badly tied reef knot
a bond is a tie or link

explanation.surface: A knot used to fasten something turns out to have been a financial asset.
explanation.walkthrough: Granny bonds were British index-linked savings certificates once sold only to pensioners; 'it was' marks them as discontinued.
explanation.definitionFit: These were UK government savings products, a form of investment aimed at older savers.

clue.text: It was a hit when the devil performed

definitions.note: a clause meaning it struck; the answer is a past-tense verb

blocks.note: an imp is a little devil
to perform on stage is to act

explanation.surface: A show was a success because the devil himself took the stage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hit' looks like a stage success, but it means struck.
explanation.definitionFit: Impacted means collided with or struck, the past tense of the verb meaning to strike forcefully.

clue.text: Legal righteousness in one could harm another

indicators.note: the letters sit in one run spread across the words that follow

blocks.note: spans the end of the first word, the second word and the start of the third

explanation.surface: Being righteous under the law in one person could still hurt someone else.
explanation.definitionFit: In Hindu and Buddhist thought, dharma is the moral law and right conduct each person must follow.

clue.text: Like a mother could lose a point and gain one - it's seriously relevant

indicators.note: losing one thing and gaining another swaps a letter in the word

blocks.note: maternal means motherly
N, north, is a compass point
Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A motherly figure might drop one argument and win another, and it really matters.
explanation.definitionFit: Material evidence is significant and pertinent, which is the legal sense of seriously relevant.

clue.text: Grabbing by the church of way-out cult

definitions.note: a gerund used as a noun; the answer is also a noun for the act of grasping, so the two match

indicators.note: way-out means wild and unconventional, so the next word's letters are disordered
the church is made of the other letters, holding them within it

blocks.note: CH is short for church
taken as written

explanation.surface: An established church seizing control of an eccentric sect.
explanation.definitionFit: A clutch is a tight grasp, the act of seizing something with the hand.

clue.text: Gaiety (and a legal term to cover it)

indicators.note: covering something wraps around it, so the term goes on the outside

blocks.note: Hilary term is one of the sittings of the English courts and Inns of Court
taken as written

explanation.surface: Merriment, with a dry aside about a legal phrase to hide it.
explanation.walkthrough: Hilary is the spring term of the English legal and university year.
explanation.definitionFit: Hilarity is loud merriment and amusement, the same lighthearted cheer that gaiety names.

clue.text: No beauty, but she was ill-used in some degree

indicators.note: ill-used suggests badly treated, so the letters of the following word are mangled
the jumbled letters sit inside the degree

blocks.note: MA is a Master of Arts degree
taken as written

explanation.surface: An unattractive woman was mistreated to some extent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'some degree' looks like 'to some extent' but supplies MA.
explanation.definitionFit: Medusa was the Gorgon of Greek myth with snakes for hair, whose face turned onlookers to stone.

clue.text: Davis run in? That's not fair

definitions.note: a person who is not fair-haired

indicators.note: putting something in places it inside the other name

blocks.note: Bette Davis was a Hollywood film star
taken as written

explanation.surface: A cricket umpire's protest when Davis is given out, or a dash for home: that's unfair!
explanation.walkthrough: 'That's not fair' sounds like a complaint, but fair here means blonde.
explanation.definitionFit: A brunette has dark brown hair, so she is not fair-haired, which is the sense of fair intended.

clue.text: Rail trip to Venetian quarter

indicators.note: to trip is to stumble, so the preceding word's letters fall into disorder

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A train journey to a district of Venice.
explanation.definitionFit: The Rialto is the commercial district of Venice around its famous bridge over the Grand Canal.

clue.text: Line taken by turbulent cleric

indicators.note: something turbulent is stirred up, so the word's letters are thrown about

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A troublesome priest takes a particular stance.
explanation.definitionFit: A circle is a closed curved line, every point an equal distance from the centre.

clue.text: Stick with present company to begin with

indicators.note: says which piece goes first in the joined word

blocks.note: Co is the abbreviation for company
present means here, in attendance

explanation.surface: Advice to stay loyal to the people around you from the outset.
explanation.definitionFit: To cohere is to hold together firmly, which is what sticking means.

clue.text: Earl without honour

definitions.note: a description of a hand of cards

blocks.note: first meaning: the Earl of ..., a British title
second meaning: a whist or bridge hand with no card higher than a nine

explanation.walkthrough: The hand is named after an earl who bet a thousand to one against being dealt it; honours are the top cards.
explanation.definitionFit: A Yarborough is a hand holding no honour cards, and the Earl of Yarborough is the peer it is named after.

clue.text: Dover, perhaps, rejecting excess of foreigners

indicators.note: rejecting suggests throwing back, so the word is turned around

blocks.note: French trop means too much, the foreigners' word for excess

explanation.surface: Dover, the English Channel gateway, turning away too many immigrants.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests immigration control, but 'excess of foreigners' is a foreign word for excess.
explanation.definitionFit: Dover is a harbour town on the Kent coast, the busiest ferry crossing point to France.

clue.text: Call for a quiet time

blocks.note: p, piano, means quiet in music
an age is a period of time

explanation.surface: A request for a peaceful moment.
explanation.definitionFit: To page someone is to summon them, by loudspeaker or pager, which is to call them.

clue.text: Laurel's pronounced averse

definitions.note: read as two words, a verse: the article joins the sound of the name and verse is the definition

indicators.note: pronounced means spoken, so the possessive name is heard rather than seen

blocks.note: Stan Laurel was the thin half of Laurel and Hardy; his name's possessive is said together with the a split off the last word

explanation.surface: Laurel is said to be reluctant, a disinclined comedian.
explanation.walkthrough: 'averse' must be split into a verse: Stan's and a, said together, become the answer, which means verse.
explanation.definitionFit: A stanza is a group of lines forming a unit of a poem, a single verse.

clue.text: In Yorkshire, Londoners make undue claim

indicators.note: Cockney Londoners famously drop their aitches, so the opening letter goes

blocks.note: Harrogate is a spa town in Yorkshire

explanation.surface: People from London living in Yorkshire make claims they aren't entitled to.
explanation.walkthrough: The town is pronounced the Cockney way, without its initial H.
explanation.definitionFit: To arrogate is to seize or claim something without justification, as a right one does not have.
